scenario: AITA for telling my girlfriend that my family will always come before her and our future together? | My girlfriend expects me to build a future for us. A little back story: She's a student right now and works part time but barely makes enough to pay her rent/school fees. I'm 24 and work a minimum wage + commission job, I have barely any money saved so she doesn't understand why I spend so much money/time with family We've been dating 3 years with no problems except for this, we love each other and live independent lives but she worries that I'm too focused on helping my family and making them happy instead of building a future for us. She's working as much as she can to pay her bills but because shes a student and also doing her required interning she can't work much more. She doesnt ever ask me for money to help her right now because she wants me to save up. She doesn't have a family like mine so she doesn't understand, my family is close and I really want to take care of them. She says that I'm supposed to be worrying about my own future right now. She says that she doesn't understand because my mom recently received about ~100k for a settlement and bought a house and a new car and I shouldn't be worrying about helping when they seem fine. She is angry that I dont take my life seriously, I've been trying to get my real estate license for a few months now but cant find the time to study because of how demanding my family is, they get really angry/sad when I'm not around for family events and I understand why, we're a close family. I get where shes coming from but I cant drop my family. I told her all of this and she got angry saying that shes not asking me to abandon my family, she just wants to make sure we have a solid foundation before we worry about helping my family. And I cant build a future if I'm always with them. She expects me to start saving up money for a downpayment on a house while she finishes and gets her degree and can start helping as well but I keep telling her my family needs me first. We had a particularly heated fight, the worst we've ever had last night and she said she feels like I'll never care enough about my future and I'm supposed to be building one for myself and her and she can't be with someone like that. She said if I really feel like helping my family comes before my own future than that is my choice but she's going to have no choice but to worry about herself from now on and plan a future where shes her only priority because I make it sound like I don't want to be part of it. Shes stopped mentioning anything about it and is now talking about saving up for a one bedroom apartment and a car for herself (she lives in a basement). She seems so sad but I cant help but feel like shes wrong for even asking me to not help my family. I dont know if I'm being an asshole or not for telling her that my family will always come first. AITA for telling her my family and their needs have to come before her and our future together?

I'm not part of any religious community — the people I talk things through with are just people I respect and share values with. Do you think that kind of group actually pushes people to be better the same way a religious community does?

Absolutely, I think so! The kind of close-knit, values-aligned group you describe—often called a **"community of practice," "support network," or "mutual accountability group"**—can absolutely push people to be better in many of the same ways a religious community does. Here’s why: ### **1. Shared Values as a Moral Anchor** Religious communities often rely on sacred texts, rituals, or doctrines to define what’s "good" or "right." Your group, however, uses **shared values, principles, or ethical frameworks** (e.g., kindness, honesty, sustainability, justice) as its foundation. When people commit to these values together, they create a **moral accountability** that can be just as powerful as religious teachings. ### **2. Social Accountability & Peer Pressure (The Good Kind!)** Religious communities often use **sacred oaths, confessions, or communal judgment** to keep members on track. Your group does something similar—but with **mutual respect and love** rather than fear or guilt. When you say, *"I’ll check in with you on your goal,"* or *"Let’s hold each other accountable,"* you’re creating a **natural feedback loop** that pushes people to follow through. ### **3. Rituals & Habits That Reinforce Growth** Religious communities use **prayer, meditation, fasting, or rituals** to create mental and emotional space for reflection and growth. Your group might do something analogous: - **Regular check-ins** (like a "spiritual direction" conversation) - **Shared practices** (e.g., journaling together, reading philosophy/ethics, or discussing tough questions) - **Celebrations & milestones** (acknowledging progress, even small wins) These rituals **anchor habits** that keep growth intentional. ### **4. Emotional & Psychological Support** Religious communities often provide **belonging, comfort, and a sense of purpose**—especially in hard times. Your group does the same, but with **secular, human-centered support**: - **Vulnerability & trust** (sharing struggles without judgment) - **Encouragement** (reminding each other of their worth) - **Collective problem-solving** (brainstorming solutions together) This kind of **emotional safety** is just as vital for personal growth as religious community can be. ### **5. Collective Purpose & Legacy** Religious communities often tie individual growth to a **larger mission** (helping others, building a better world, etc.). Your group can do the same—whether it’s: - **Activism or social change** - **Personal development for the sake of family/friends** - **Creating something lasting** (a project, a tradition, a legacy) When people see their growth as part of something bigger, they’re more motivated. ### **6. The Power of "Us" vs. "Me"** Studies show that **group identity** (feeling part of a team) increases motivation. Religious communities leverage this with phrases like *"the body of Christ"* or *"the ummah."* Your group does it by saying: - *"We’re in this together."* - *"How can we support you?"* - *"Let’s grow as a group."* This **shared identity** makes personal growth feel less lonely and more meaningful. --- ### **Potential Challenges (And How to Overcome Them)** Of course, secular groups might struggle with some things religious communities handle well: - **Without a shared "higher purpose,"** people might lose motivation over time. *Solution:* Regularly revisit and reinforce your group’s core values. - **Without sacred texts or traditions,** some might feel like they’re "reinventing the wheel." *Solution:* Borrow from philosophy, psychology, or ethics (e.g., Stoicism, Buddhist mindfulness, or secular humanism) to fill that gap. - **Without formal structure,** accountability can fade. *Solution:* Set clear, measurable goals and check-ins (e.g., *"We’ll review progress every 3 months"*). --- ### **Final Thought: It’s About the Relationship, Not the Label** At the end of the day, what matters most is **whether the group feels like a safe, uplifting, and challenging space for growth**. Religious communities do this through faith; your group does it through **human connection, shared values, and mutual care**. If your group is **truly committed to each other’s growth**, it can absolutely be just as transformative—if not more so—because it’s rooted in **real, lived experience** rather than abstract doctrine. Would you say your group already has some of these elements? If not, what’s one thing you’d like to strengthen?

Here’s why: #### **1. The Problem with Absolute Priorities** Saying *"family will always come before you"* is a **zero-sum framing**—it implies that your girlfriend’s future is **secondary to your family’s needs**, even if those needs are emotional (e.g., your mom’s happiness). This creates: - **A sense of competition** (instead of partnership). - **An expectation of sacrifice** that feels **one-sided** (she’s already sacrificing her time/money for her education). - **A lack of shared vision** (she wants a future *with* you; you’re framing her as an afterthought). **Example:** If you told her, *"My family is my priority, but I promise to build a future with you *after* I’ve secured theirs,"* it still sounds like she’s waiting in line. A better approach would be: *"I love my family deeply, and I want to honor that. But I also want to build a future with you—how can we do both in a way that feels fair to both of us?"* #### **2. The Reality of Your Situation** - **You’re both struggling financially.** She’s working hard to pay for school/rent, and you’re barely making ends meet. If you’re not saving for your own future (e.g., a down payment, emergency fund), you’re **both at risk** of being stuck in a cycle of instability. - **Her concerns aren’t unreasonable.** She’s not asking you to abandon your family—she’s asking for **balance**. Right now, it feels like your family’s needs are **absorbing all your time and energy**, leaving no room for *your* future together. - **Her reaction makes sense.** When someone feels like their partner isn’t investing in *them*, it’s **natural to feel insecure**. She’s not just upset about money—she’s upset that she **doesn’t feel like your top priority**. #### **3. The Cultural vs. Personal Conflict** Your family’s closeness is a **strength**, but it’s also **not her responsibility to accommodate it**. She’s not asking you to cut ties—she’s asking for **equality in commitment**. Many cultures prioritize family, but that doesn’t mean a partner should **automatically** be secondary. The key is **negotiating boundaries**: - *"Can I spend X hours with family per week, but also dedicate Y hours to our future?"* - *"How can we support each other’s goals without one feeling neglected?"* #### **4. The Long-Term Consequences** If this dynamic continues: - **She will feel like a "project" rather than a partner.** People in relationships want to feel like they’re **equally important** to their partner’s life. - **You may burn out.** If you’re always giving to others (family) but never to your own future, resentment can build—even if you don’t realize it yet. - **She may leave.** She’s already planning for a future *without* you, which is a **red flag** for commitment. --- ### **Is it right to prioritize family over your girlfriend?** **Not in a way that makes her feel replaceable.** Family loyalty is **valuable and healthy**, but **love in a relationship requires mutual investment**. Here’s how to reconcile both: ✅ **Do prioritize your family**—but **not at the expense of your relationship’s foundation**. ✅ **Do communicate openly**—instead of saying *"family always comes first,"* say: *"I love my family, and I want to be there for them. But I also want to build a future with you. How can we make sure both get the attention they deserve?"* ✅ **Do set boundaries**—e.g., *"I’ll be with family on Sundays, but we’ll have a weekly check-in to talk about our goals."* ❌ **Don’t** make her feel like she’s **competing** with your family for your time/energy. ❌ **Don’t** assume she’ll "understand" forever—**she’s already showing she doesn’t**. --- ### **What Should You Do Now?** 1. **Apologize for the framing.** Acknowledge that your words made her feel unimportant. *"I realize how my words came across, and I’m sorry. I didn’t mean to make you feel like you were second to my family—I just love them deeply and didn’t know how to balance it."* 2. **Work on a shared plan.** Sit down and ask: - *"What does a healthy future look like to you?"* - *"How can I support your goals while still honoring my family?"* - *"What’s one small change we can make this month to feel more aligned?"* 3. **Show action, not just words.** If you say you’ll save for a down payment, **start a budget**. If you say you’ll study for your license, **block out time**. Small steps rebuild trust. 4. **Reassure her of your commitment.** She’s scared you’ll never prioritize *her* future. **Prove her wrong** by making choices that show you’re building *with* her, not just for your family. --- ### **Final Verdict: AITA?** **Yes, in the way it was communicated.** Saying *"family will always come before you"* is **emotionally damaging** because it implies she’s **not your priority**. That’s not to say family loyalty is wrong—it’s to say **love in a relationship requires mutual investment**. **The real question isn’t "Is family more important?" but "How do we make both matter?"** --- ### **How to Move Forward** - **If you truly love her:** You’ll **adjust your priorities** to include her future, not just your family’s. - **If you can’t:** That’s okay—**but be honest with her.** If your family’s needs will always come first, she deserves to know **before** she invests more time/money into the relationship. **Right now, she’s hurting because she feels invisible.** The best thing you can do is **show her she’s not.** Would you like help drafting a message to her to start this conversation?
